title: Habsburg: from a castle in the Aargau to an empire
card: How a noble family from the Aargau became kings, lost its Swiss lands to the Confederates, and ruled half of Europe.

stops.title: A castle above the Aare
text: About 1020 a noble family builds a castle on a hill above the Aare river, in today's Aargau. The builder was Radbot or Werner. The castle is called Habsburg, and the family takes its name.
Soon after, Radbot founds the abbey of Muri. The family owns farms and rights around the castle and Muri. At first it is one noble family among many in the region.

stops.title: Count rights after Lenzburg
text: In 1172–1173 the counts of Lenzburg die out. The Habsburgs get part of their rights: the county (high court) in the Aargau and in the western Zürichgau, which includes Schwyz and Unterwalden. They also become protectors of Säckingen abbey.
The counts of Kyburg get another part. Kyburg and Habsburg are now neighbours and rivals in northern Switzerland.

stops.title: The Kyburg inheritance
text: In 1263 and 1264 the last two counts of Kyburg die. Count Rudolf of Habsburg is their nearest heir. He takes over their lands in the east: the Winterthur area, the Thurgau, Baden, Glarus and Zug.

In the west, Burgdorf and Thun go to Anna, the young daughter of the last count. Rudolf rules these lands for her. Rudolf is now the strongest lord between the Rhine and the Alps. Only a few towns and valleys stand directly under the king: for example Zurich, Bern, Uri and Schwyz.

stops.title: A king and a duchy
text: In 1273 the princes elect Count Rudolf as king of the Romans (the German king). In 1278 he defeats King Ottokar of Bohemia at Dürnkrut, north-east of Vienna. Ottokar dies in the battle.

In 1282 Rudolf gives the duchies of Austria and Styria to his sons. From now on the Habsburgs are dukes of Austria. Their centre of power moves east to Vienna, but they keep their old lands in Switzerland and in Alsace.

stops.title: Habsburg and the forest valleys
text: Rudolf and his sons want to join their Swiss lands into one territory. In 1291 they buy the rights of Murbach abbey over Lucerne. They also protect the abbeys of Engelberg and Einsiedeln.

Uri and Schwyz have letters from earlier kings that put them directly under the Empire. They fear Habsburg rule. After Rudolf dies in July 1291, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden (Nidwalden) renew their alliance.

stops.title: Morgarten, Sempach, Näfels
text: The Habsburgs try several times to force the valleys and towns under their rule. In 1315 the men of Schwyz beat a Habsburg army at Morgarten. Historians today argue about how big this battle really was.

Lucerne (1332), Zurich (1351), Glarus and Zug (1352) and Bern (1353) join the alliance. In 1386 the Confederates beat Duke Leopold III at Sempach. He dies in the battle. In 1388 Glarus wins at Näfels.
Habsburg loses Lucerne, Zug and Glarus. It keeps the Aargau, the Thurgau and much of the countryside.

stops.title: The Aargau is lost
text: In 1415 Duke Frederick IV of Austria helps Pope John XXIII flee from the Council of Constance. King Sigismund puts the duke under the ban of the Empire and asks his neighbours to take his lands.

The Confederates conquer the Aargau in about a month. Bern, Lucerne and Zurich each take a part. Baden and the Free Offices become common lordships (land ruled jointly by several cantons). The old Habsburg castle is now Swiss.
Habsburg keeps the Fricktal, the Thurgau and Fribourg. Rapperswil becomes a free imperial town in 1415, but is Habsburg again from 1442 to 1458.

stops.title: The Thurgau is lost
text: Duke Sigismund of Tyrol quarrels with Nicholas of Cusa, the bishop of Brixen. In 1460 the pope puts Sigismund under the ban of the church. The Confederates use this and take the Thurgau. It becomes a common lordship of seven cantons.
Fribourg leaves Habsburg in 1452, and Rapperswil in 1458–1460. Winterthur goes to Zurich in 1467. South of the Rhine, only the Fricktal stays with Austria.

stops.title: Peace: the Ewige Richtung
text: In 1469 Sigismund pledges his lands in Alsace and on the Upper Rhine to Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy. Soon Charles becomes a danger to both Austria and the Swiss.

In 1474 Sigismund and the Confederates make the Ewige Richtung (perpetual settlement) at Constance. Each side keeps the land it holds, so the Aargau and Thurgau stay Swiss. Old enemies become partners against Burgundy.

stops.title: The Swabian War
text: King Maximilian I wants the Empire to have a common tax and a new imperial court. The Swiss do not accept them, and there are border quarrels. In 1499 war breaks out between the Confederates with the Grisons on one side, and Maximilian with the Swabian League (an alliance of south German lords and towns) on the other.

The Swiss win at Calven and at Dornach. In the Peace of Basel (22 September 1499) the Swiss gain only the Thurgau high court. But after 1499 the Empire's courts and taxes no longer reach the Swiss in practice.
In 1511 Austria and the Swiss sign a hereditary union (Erbeinung). They promise to respect each other's land.

stops.title: An empire around Switzerland
text: Maximilian's grandson Charles V becomes king of Spain in 1516 and emperor in 1519. With Spain come Naples, Sicily, Sardinia and lands in America. In 1535 he also takes the Duchy of Milan. About 1550 Habsburg land lies north, east and south of the Swiss. In 1556 the family splits into a Spanish line and an Austrian line. The family that began at a small castle in the Aargau is now one of the great powers of Europe.

title: Savoy: masters of the Alpine passes and the Vaud
card: How the counts of Savoy took the Vaud and the passes, lost them to Bern and the Valais, and became kings in Turin.

stops.title: Counts of the Alpine passes
text: The house of Savoy begins in the early 1000s with Count Humbert. His family lands lie mostly in the Bugey and the Grésivaudan (the Isère valley).

His son Odo marries Adelaide, daughter of the margrave of Turin. This brings the Susa valley and Piedmont. Now Savoy holds both sides of the passes, for example Mont-Cenis and the Great St Bernard. Tolls and travellers on these roads bring money and power.
Early on the family also gains the Chablais, the land around the old abbey of Saint-Maurice.

stops.title: Peter II and the Vaud
text: Peter of Savoy (about 1203–1268) is the seventh son of Count Thomas I. At first he is meant for a career in the Church. Later he builds his own power north of Lake Geneva. Between 1240 and 1260 he forces many nobles of the Vaud to hold their land from him as a fief (land held in return for loyalty).

He beats the count of Geneva and pushes back the bishop of Lausanne. In 1260 a treaty with the bishop of Sion gives him the land down to the Morge stream near Conthey. Bern and Murten seek his protection in the 1250s.
Peter becomes count of Savoy in 1263. A chronicle of 1419 calls him the 'little Charlemagne'.

stops.title: The Duchy of Savoy
text: From 1285 a side line of the family holds the Vaud. In 1359 Count Amadeus VI takes it back.

The duchy now reaches from the Swiss plateau to the Mediterranean.

sources.quote: Als Karl II. 1536 versuchte, Genf einzunehmen, reagierte Bern mit einem erneuten Einmarsch ins Waadtland sowie ins Pays de Gex und das Genevois.

stops.title: A new state around Turin
text: Duke Emmanuel Philibert gets most of his lands back in 1559. In 1563 he makes Turin his capital. The duchy now looks south, to Italy.

In the Treaty of Lausanne (1564) and at Thonon (1569) he makes peace with Bern and the Valais. He gets back the land south of Lake Geneva. In return, the Vaud stays Bernese, and the Valais keeps the Monthey area. These borders still hold today.

In 1713 the duke becomes king of Sicily. In 1720 he swaps Sicily for Sardinia. His state is now called the Kingdom of Sardinia, but its centre is still Turin and Piedmont.

In 1860 Savoy and Nice become French. This is France's reward for helping the king of Sardinia in the war to unite Italy. From 1861 the family rules the Kingdom of Italy, until 1946.

title: The Zähringen and the Kyburg: lords who built towns
card: Two families founded many Swiss towns, then died out within fifty years and left their land to Habsburg and the free towns.

stops.title: Dukes from the Breisgau
text: The Zähringen family are counts in the Breisgau, the land around today's Freiburg in Germany. From 1092 to 1098 they are rival dukes of Swabia.
In 1098 they make peace. Berchtold II gives up Swabia. In return he gets the castle of Zähringen and the king's rights in Zurich. From now on the family calls itself dukes of Zähringen.

Around 1065–1070 the counts of Dillingen, from the Danube, get a foothold in northern Switzerland. By a marriage they get large lands in the Thurgau and claims around Winterthur. From 1180 a branch of the family calls itself counts of Kyburg.

stops.title: Rectors of Burgundy
text: In 1127 King Lothar III makes Duke Konrad rector of Burgundy. A rector rules a land in the king's name. In practice Konrad can enforce this only between the Jura, Lake Geneva and the Alps.

Even there the dukes are strong only in parts of it. The local nobles avoid serving them. In 1156 Duke Berchtold IV must give up his hopes for the rest of Burgundy. Instead the emperor gives him the right to give the bishops of Geneva, Lausanne and Sion their worldly rights. The duke can enforce this only in Lausanne.

stops.title: Fribourg is founded
text: In 1157 Duke Berchtold IV founds the town of Fribourg on the Saane river. It has the same name as the family's town in the Breisgau.

In 1156 the duke lost much of his power in western Switzerland. With the new town he tries to build his own power base between the Aare and the Saane. The site is easy to defend and lies on good roads.

stops.title: Bern and a ring of towns
text: In 1173 the counts of Lenzburg die out. The Zähringen, the Kyburg and the Habsburg all gain from it. The Kyburg get land near Baden and around the Walensee.

In 1190–1191 Duke Berchtold V beats the nobles and the bishop of Lausanne, who rise against him. There are fights at Payerne and Grindelwald. In 1191 he finishes the founding of Bern and builds up the town of Thun. The Zähringen also build up Burgdorf, Murten and Moudon, and castle settlements such as Laupen. In 1198 King Philip gives the duke the imperial rights over Schaffhausen.
Historians think that only Fribourg and Bern were real towns before 1218.

stops.title: The Zähringen die out
text: Duke Berchtold V dies in 1218 without a son. King Frederick II takes back the title of duke and most of the imperial rights.

Bern, Zurich, Solothurn and Schaffhausen now stand directly under the Empire. The family's own lands are split. The counts of Urach get the land north of the Rhine. The counts of Kyburg get Fribourg, Burgdorf, Thun and land in the Aargau and around Zurich. Count Ulrich III of Kyburg had married Anna of Zähringen, of the duke's family.

stops.title: Kyburg at its height
text: The counts of Kyburg now rule a broad belt of land from Zurich and the Thurgau to Fribourg. Like the Zähringen, they found towns to hold it: Winterthur and Diessenhofen about 1180, Zug and Baden about 1230, later Frauenfeld, Aarau, Mellingen and Lenzburg, and about 1250 Sursee and Weesen.
In 1250–1251 the family splits its land. Hartmann IV keeps the east. His nephew Hartmann V gets the west, with Burgdorf as its centre, and Thun and Fribourg. Neither has a son.

stops.title: Habsburg takes the Kyburg land
text: Hartmann V dies in 1263 and Hartmann IV one year later. Count Rudolf of Habsburg is a nephew of Hartmann IV. As guardian of Hartmann V's young daughter Anna he runs the western lands. From 1264 to 1273 he also runs the rest of the Kyburg land.

About 1273 Anna marries Eberhard of Habsburg-Laufenburg. Their line, called Neu-Kyburg, holds Burgdorf and Thun. It sells them to Bern in 1384 and dies out in 1417. In 1277 Rudolf, now king, makes the Kyburg heirs sell Fribourg to his sons. The rest of the Kyburg land becomes the base of Habsburg power in eastern Switzerland.

title: Bishops and abbeys as lords
card: Between 950 and 1300, kings gave counties to bishops and abbeys, who ruled much of today's Switzerland before Savoy and Habsburg pushed them back.

stops.title: Two realms meet
text: About 950 today's Switzerland is split between two realms. The west belongs to the Kingdom of Burgundy. Its kings, the Rudolfings, began in 888 with Rudolf I, who was chosen king at Saint-Maurice.

The east belongs to the Duchy of Swabia, a part of the German kingdom. Its land reaches from the Upper Rhine and the Aare to the Lech river, and includes Rhaetia (today's Grisons). Zurich is one of the dukes' main seats. The border between the two realms runs roughly along the Aare.
The south (today's Ticino) belongs to the Kingdom of Italy.

stops.title: The bishop of Chur
text: Kings like to give power to bishops. A bishop cannot pass land to a son, so the land stays with the church, and the king can choose the next bishop.

Between 951 and 960 King Otto I gives Bishop Hartpert of Chur income from the county, the tolls of Chur, the right to make coins (958) and rights in the Bergell. This is the start of the bishop's rule over Chur and the roads to the Alpine passes.
The abbey of Disentis, founded in the 700s, holds the upper Rhine valley below the Lukmanier and Oberalp passes.

stops.title: Sion and Basel get counties
text: King Rudolf III of Burgundy is weak against his nobles. To build a counterweight, he gives counties to the church. In 999 he gives the bishop of Sion the County of Valais with all its rights.

In the same year he gives the old abbey of Moutier-Grandval to the bishop of Basel. Before this, the bishop ruled little outside his city. Now he holds land in the Jura from Lake Biel to Alsace. This is the start of the Prince-Bishopric of Basel.

stops.title: Abbeys as lords
text: Abbeys also rule land and people. St. Gallen (founded in the 700s) holds land around the town and in Appenzell. Einsiedeln (934) owns much of the valley around it. Engelberg (1120) owns its own valley. Disentis holds the upper Rhine valley and Urseren.
Other abbeys own manors far away. The Fraumünster in Zurich owned land in Uri and at Cham. Lucerne depends on Murbach abbey in Alsace.
Like bishops, abbeys need protectors. Kyburg, Habsburg and others take these posts and use them to build their own power.

stops.title: Church land under pressure
text: By 1300 big lay lords press the church lords. Savoy takes most of the Vaud from the bishop of Lausanne. In the Valais, Savoy pushes into the bishop of Sion's lands. Habsburg protects Engelberg (1274) and Einsiedeln, and in 1291 buys Murbach's rights in Lucerne.

Some church lords stay strong. About 1300 the bishop of Basel is at the height of his power; in 1305 he buys Liestal and Waldenburg in today's Baselland, but soon loses them. The abbey of St. Gallen holds land in Appenzell, and the bishop of Chur rules wide lands in the Grisons. Several of these church states last until 1798.

sources.supports: Savoy also presses the bishop of Geneva about 1300.

sources.title: HLS: Chur (Diözese, Fürstbistum)
sources.quote: Zu den Vasallen und Ministerialen des Fürstbischofs gehörten die mächtigsten rätischen Familien.
sources.supports: The bishop of Chur is a leading lord in the Grisons (his lands: Chur, Bergell, Oberhalbstein, Engadin, Domleschg...).

sources.title: HLS: Waadt
sources.quote: Aber erst dessen Sohn Peter II. nahm die Waadt eigentlich in Besitz, indem er 1240-1260 systematisch Feudalrechte erwarb
sources.supports: Savoy takes most of the Vaud from the bishop of Lausanne

sources.title: HLS: Engelberg (Kloster)
sources.quote: nahm König Rudolf I. von Habsburg 1274 das Kloster in seinen Schutz.
sources.supports: Habsburg protects Engelberg from 1274

sources.title: HLS: Morgartenkrieg
sources.quote: dem schwyzerischen Überfall auf das unter österreichischer Schirmvogtei stehende Kloster
sources.supports: Habsburg (Austria) protects Einsiedeln

sources.title: HLS: Habsburg, von
sources.quote: kaufte 1291 die Grundherrschaft über die Höfe des Klosters Murbach-Luzern.
sources.supports: In 1291 Habsburg buys Murbach's rights in Lucerne

sources.title: HLS: Basel (Fürstbistum)
sources.quote: durch den Kauf der Herrschaften Liestal, Neu-Homberg und Waldenburg für 2100 Mark Silber im Jahr 1305.
sources.supports: In 1305 the bishop of Basel buys Liestal and Waldenburg

sources.title: HLS: Basel (Fürstbistum)
sources.quote: so entgingen diese Herrschaften schliesslich dem Fürstbistum Basel.
sources.supports: He soon loses them (corrects the old text)

sources.title: HLS: Basel (Fürstbistum)
sources.quote: Zu Beginn des 14. Jahrhunderts stand das Fürstbistum Basel auf dem Höhepunkt seiner Macht.
sources.supports: About 1300 the bishop of Basel is at the height of his power

sources.title: HLS: St. Gallen (Fürstabtei)
sources.quote: Zusammen bildeten sie auch das Kerngebiet der Klosterherrschaft um 1300.
sources.supports: St. Gallen holds land in Appenzell about 1300

sources.title: HLS: Graubünden
sources.quote: Chur die ausgedehnteste; sie umfasste seit ottonischer Zeit, neben Stadt und Umland Chur, das Bergell
sources.supports: The bishop of Chur rules wide lands in the Grisons

uncertain: Map: the bishop of Constance holds Neunkirch and Hallau (from 1302).

notes: The Burgundy–Swabia border is drawn along today's Bernese districts as a rough Aare line; Basel is counted as Burgundian about 950 (it belonged to Burgundy for part of the 10th century). Outside Switzerland Burgundy is drawn as whole French départements from the Franche-Comté to Provence plus Aosta; Swabia as Baden-Württemberg, Alsace and Vorarlberg (Bavarian Swabia not drawn). The Lausanne county of 1011 is drawn as all of today's Vaud. Bishop of Basel lands about 1200 drawn as all of Jura plus Moutier-Grandval (rough). St. Gallen and Chur lands are approximate. Foundation dates: St. Gallen and Disentis given only as 'the 700s'.
